name: Delphi
title: Modern Delphi: Object Pascal today
intro: Delphi is still developed and sold today by Embarcadero, as the successor of the Borland line. It builds native programs for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS from one Object Pascal code base, with the VCL for Windows and FireMonkey for the other platforms. The language has grown a lot since Delphi 7: Unicode strings with helper methods, generics and collections, records with methods, for ... in loops, anonymous methods and inline variables. This course teaches the current language with small console programs. If you want the classic Delphi 5, 6 and 7, that course is in the older section. To run a program yourself, make a new console application in Delphi (the free Community Edition is enough) and paste the code in.

lessons.title: A modern console program
lessons.summary: program, uses System.SysUtils, Writeln and Unicode strings.

sections.p: A console program starts with program, asks for a console window with {$APPTYPE CONSOLE}, and lists the units it needs after uses. Units today have namespaced names such as System.SysUtils; Delphi 7 just said SysUtils. The code runs between begin and end. (with a full stop).
Since Delphi 2009, string is a Unicode string, so any language's text fits in it. Length counts UTF-16 code units, and s[1] is still the first character: the classic functions count from 1.

practice.why: Format replaces each %s with a string and each %d with an integer, in order.
S[1] is the first character, and Length gives 5. Writeln prints the items side by side.
Borland's tools passed to CodeGear and then to Embarcadero, which still releases new versions.

options: The namespaced name of the SysUtils unit
practice.answer: The namespaced name of the SysUtils unit
practice.why: Modern Delphi groups its units into namespaces such as System, Vcl and FMX.

lessons.title: String helpers
lessons.summary: Methods on strings, and why they count from 0.

sections.p: Modern Delphi lets you call methods on a string directly: S.ToUpper, S.Contains, S.Replace, S.Split. These come from a record helper for string in System.SysUtils.
sections.out:
HAZELNUT
True
Hazeltree
oak, elm, ash

sections.p: Watch out: the helper methods use 0-based positions, like most other languages, while the classic functions such as Pos and Copy and the S[i] index count from 1. S.IndexOf returns -1 when nothing is found, where Pos returns 0.

practice.why: Helper methods count from 0, so S is at 0 and q is at 1.
Pos is a classic function and counts from 1.
Replace changes every match, not just the first one.

practice.q: What does S.IndexOf return when the text is not found?
practice.why: 0 is a real position for a 0-based method, so not-found is -1. Pos, which counts from 1, uses 0 instead.

lessons.title: Records with methods
lessons.summary: Advanced records: fields, methods and constructors.

sections.p: A record can have methods and constructors, not just fields. Records are value types: assigning one copies it, and there is nothing to free. They suit small things such as points, money amounts and dates.

practice.why: Records are copied on assignment, so changing B leaves A alone.

practice.q: Do you need to Free a record?
practice.why: Records live where they are declared and go away by themselves. Class instances are the ones you free.

practice.q: What is Result inside a function?
options: A keyword that ends the function
practice.why: Assign to Result to set the return value. Unlike Exit, it does not leave the function.

lessons.title: Classes and properties
lessons.summary: Constructors, properties, try...finally and virtual methods.

sections.p: A class instance lives on the heap, so you create it and free it yourself. The standard pattern puts Free in a try ... finally block, so it runs even if something goes wrong. A property looks like a field to the caller but can go through a method.
A class can extend another. Mark a method virtual in the parent and override in the child, and the right version is chosen by the object's real class at run time.

practice.why: The object is a TChild, so its override runs, and inherited Name calls the parent's version.

practice.q: Why put Free in a finally block?
options: So the object is freed even if an exception happens
practice.answer: So the object is freed even if an exception happens
practice.why: The finally part always runs, whether the try part finishes normally or raises an exception.

practice.q: What does a property with a write method let you do?
options: Check or change a value as it is set
Stop the value from being read
practice.answer: Check or change a value as it is set
practice.why: Assigning to the property calls the setter, which can validate the value, as SetNuts does.

lessons.title: Generics and collections
lessons.summary: TList<T>, TDictionary<K, V> and for ... in.

sections.p: System.Generics.Collections has type-safe collections. TList<Integer> is a growable list of integers, and for X in List do walks through it. Collections are classes, so they are freed in a finally.

TDictionary<string, Integer> maps keys to values. TryGetValue looks a key up without raising an exception when it is missing. A dictionary keeps no particular order, so do not rely on the order of a for ... in over it.

practice.why: A TList is indexed from 0, so L[1] is the second item added.
Sort puts the list in ascending order before the loop prints it.

practice.q: What does the <Integer> in TList<Integer> do?
options: Says the list only holds integers, checked by the compiler
practice.answer: Says the list only holds integers, checked by the compiler
practice.why: That is a generic type argument. Adding a string to a TList<Integer> will not compile.

lessons.title: Exceptions
lessons.summary: try...except, raise and your own exception classes.

sections.p: raise throws an exception object, and try ... except on E: SomeClass do catches it. Make your own exception classes by inheriting from Exception. The first matching on branch wins, so put specific classes before general ones.
sections.out:
Ate one, 0 left
Caught: The stash is empty

practice.why: raise jumps straight to the except block, so C is skipped. After the except block the program carries on with D.
The finally block runs first, while the exception passes through, and then the outer except catches it.

practice.q: How do you declare your own exception class?
practice.why: An exception is a class that inherits from Exception. The E prefix is the usual naming habit.

lessons.title: Newer syntax
lessons.summary: Inline variables, type inference and anonymous methods.

sections.p: These features are reading material: they need a current Delphi compiler, so the examples have no output shown here.

Since Delphi 10.3 you can declare a variable where you first need it, inside begin ... end, instead of in a var block at the top. The type can be left out when it is clear from the value, and a loop counter can be declared right in the for. An inline variable only exists inside the block where it is declared.

An anonymous method is a procedure or function without a name, written right where it is used, and it can use the variables around it. Its type is written reference to function .... They are used for callbacks, sorting rules and background tasks.

practice.q: Where can an inline variable be used?
options: Only inside the block where it is declared
practice.answer: Only inside the block where it is declared
practice.why: Inline variables are scoped to their begin...end block, which keeps them close to where they are used.

practice.q: What type does var Count := 3; give Count?
practice.why: With type inference the compiler takes the type from the value, and 3 is an Integer.

practice.q: What can an anonymous method use that a plain procedure cannot?
options: Local variables from where it was written
practice.answer: Local variables from where it was written
practice.why: It captures the variables around it. In MakeAdder, the returned function keeps Amount after MakeAdder has returned.

lessons.title: Enumerations, sets and case
lessons.summary: Naming a fixed list of choices, and holding several at once.

sections.p: An enumerated type lists every value a variable may hold, with names instead of magic numbers. Ord gives a value's position (from 0), Succ and Pred step to the next and previous, and Low/High give the first and last, so a for loop can visit them all. A case statement picks a branch for each value.
sections.out:
0 spring: find food
1 summer: find food
2 autumn: bury nuts
3 winter: dig them up
after autumn comes winter

sections.p: A set holds any combination of values from a small ordinal type, such as an enumeration or the letters. in tests membership, + joins two sets, * keeps what they share and - removes. Include and Exclude change a set in place. Pascal has had sets since the 1970s; they are a compact, readable way to keep flags.
sections.out:
both like: walnut
either likes: acorn hazelnut walnut beechnut
only Sam: acorn beechnut
Pip likes chestnuts: TRUE
u is a vowel: TRUE

practice.why: Positions start at 0, so Large is 2, and Succ(Small) is Medium, which is 1.
A * B is [3, 4], which holds 3. A - B is [1, 2], which does not hold 5.

practice.q: Why use an enumerated type instead of plain integers 0 to 3?
options: The names make the code readable and the compiler rejects values outside the list
Integers cannot be used in case statements
practice.answer: The names make the code readable and the compiler rejects values outside the list
practice.why: TSeason can only ever be one of its four names, and the code says which.

lessons.title: Dynamic arrays and open arrays
lessons.summary: Arrays whose size is set while the program runs.

sections.p: A dynamic array, declared as array of Integer, has no fixed size. SetLength gives it room (new elements start at 0) and can grow it later, keeping what is there. Indexes run from 0 to High(A), and Length gives the count. Delphi frees the memory itself when the array is no longer used.

A parameter written const Values: array of Integer is an open array: the routine accepts a static array, a dynamic array, or a list written in place in square brackets. Inside, it is indexed from 0 to High(Values). That is how Format takes its list of arguments.

Dynamic arrays are reference types: assigning one to another makes both names share the same elements. Copy makes an independent copy, and it can take just a slice: Copy(A, 1, 2) is two elements starting at index 1.

practice.why: New elements start at 0, growing keeps A[1], and High of a 4-element array is 3.
The open array takes the list in brackets, and the loop adds every element.

practice.q: After B := A with two dynamic arrays, what happens when you change B[0]?
options: A[0] changes too, because they share the elements
practice.answer: A[0] changes too, because they share the elements
practice.why: Use Copy(A) when you need an independent array.

lessons.title: Interfaces
lessons.summary: Promises a class keeps, and objects that free themselves.

sections.p: An interface lists methods without any code. A class that names the interface promises to provide them, and code written against the interface works with every such class. Classes that implement interfaces usually inherit from TInterfacedObject, which does the bookkeeping. Describe takes its parameter without const on purpose: a brand-new object passed straight into a const interface parameter is never counted, so it is never freed.
sections.out:
tree hollow holds 120
burrow 30 cm deep holds 60

sections.p: Objects used through an interface variable are reference counted: Delphi counts how many interface variables point at the object and frees it when the count drops to zero. So, unlike ordinary objects, you do not call Free and need no try ... finally. Do not mix the two styles for one object: keep it in interface variables only.
sections.out:
create Sam
A cleared
hello from Sam
free Sam
B cleared

practice.q: When is an object used only through interface variables freed?
options: When the last interface variable pointing at it is cleared or goes out of scope
practice.answer: When the last interface variable pointing at it is cleared or goes out of scope
practice.why: TInterfacedObject counts the references and frees itself at zero.

practice.q: What does an interface declaration contain?
options: Method headings only, with no code
practice.answer: Method headings only, with no code
practice.why: The classes that implement it supply the code.
N.Value calls TTwo's method, which returns 2.

lessons.title: Text and files with TStringList
lessons.summary: Lists of lines that can be sorted, saved and loaded.

sections.p: TStringList from System.Classes is a list of strings with handy extras: Sort, IndexOf, SaveToFile and LoadFromFile. It is a class, so create it, use it inside try, and free it in finally.
sections.out:
sorted: beech,hazel,oak
hazel is at 1
1. beech
2. hazel
3. oak

sections.p: A TStringList also understands lines of the form name=value, which makes a simple settings file. Values['name'] reads or sets a value, and an unknown name gives an empty string. StrToIntDef converts text to a number with a fallback for bad input.
sections.out:
Sam keeps 50 nuts
missing: ""
-1
name=Sam
nuts=50
tree=oak

practice.why: Sort puts "ash" first, and the list holds two lines.

practice.q: Why is a TStringList freed in a finally block?
options: It is a class, so it must be freed even if an exception happens
Strings are freed only in finally
practice.answer: It is a class, so it must be freed even if an exception happens
practice.why: Ordinary objects are not reference counted; try ... finally guarantees Free runs.
'12' converts to 12; 'x' is not a number, so the default 5 is used.

lessons.title: Project: a nut report
lessons.summary: Records, enums, dynamic arrays and Format in one program.

sections.p: This program stores a season of finds as an array of records, adds them up per kind of nut with an array indexed by an enumeration, finds the best day, and prints a report with Format. In Format, %-9s left-aligns text in 9 columns and %4d right-aligns a number in 4; %5.1f prints a real number with one decimal.
sections.out:
acorn      18  72.0%
hazelnut    6  24.0%
walnut      1   4.0%
total      25
best single find: 9 on day 3

sections.p: Save the finds to a file with a TStringList (one day,nut,count line each) and load them back, turn TFind into a record with a ToString method, or replace the array of totals with a TDictionary<string, Integer> so new kinds of nut need no change to the type.

practice.why: A minus sign left-aligns; without it the value is right-aligned in the width.

practice.q: Why can Totals be declared as array[TNut] of Integer?
options: An enumeration can be used as an array's index type
practice.answer: An enumeration can be used as an array's index type
practice.why: There is exactly one element per kind of nut, and Totals[Walnut] reads naturally.
Inc(X) adds 1, and Inc(X, N) adds N.
